title: Valuation Integrity: When a Judgement Becomes a Payment
summary: One turn of multiple moved accrued carry from 4 to 20 — and both marks were defensible, which is exactly why the process matters more than the number.

lesson.body:
In private markets the manager values its own portfolio, and those valuations determine reported performance, fundraising success, [[management-fee|management fees]] in some structures, and accrued [[carried-interest|carry]].

**That is not a scandal. It is the structure, because there is no market price to use instead.** A private company has no quoted value, so someone has to estimate one, and the person with the most information is the owner.

What makes it work or fail is the process around the judgement:

**Who prepares the valuation** and whether they are compensated on its level.

**Who reviews it** — an independent committee, a third-party valuation firm, an auditor, or nobody.

**Whether the methodology is fixed in advance** and applied consistently, or chosen each quarter.

**Whether changes are documented** with reasons, so a pattern is visible.

**The ethical content is entirely in the process**, because the number itself is genuinely uncertain and two honest people can differ by a wide margin. **Which means "the mark is defensible" is true and insufficient — the question is whether the same process would have produced a lower number when a lower number was the honest answer.**

**A small change in a valuation produces a large change in accrued carry, because carry is charged on the gain rather than on the value.**

The arithmetic is worth doing once carefully.

A portfolio company with 80 of [[ebitda|EBITDA]] and 400 of debt. At **9x** the [[enterprise-value|enterprise value]] is 720 and the equity is **320**. At **10x** it is 800 and **400**. One turn of multiple, 80 of equity value, **25% higher**.

Now put it in a fund. The fund cost 1,000; the rest of the portfolio is held at cost, 700.

- **At 9x:** NAV = 700 + 320 = **1,020**. Gain over cost = **20**. Accrued carry at 20% = **4.0**.
- **At 10x:** NAV = 700 + 400 = **1,100**. Gain over cost = **100**. Accrued carry at 20% = **20.0**.

**One turn of multiple on one holding moved accrued carry from 4 to 20 — a fivefold change.**

The reason is that carry sits above a threshold, so it is levered to the gain. Near the point where the fund crosses from no carry to carry, **the sensitivity of the manager's compensation to a valuation judgement is extreme.**

This is not an accusation. **It is a structural fact that explains why valuation governance exists, and why it should be strongest exactly when a fund is near its hurdle.** A process that is adequate in normal circumstances is being tested hardest at the moment it matters most.

**The realistic failure is not a fabricated valuation. It is drift: a long series of small, defensible choices that all point the same way.**

Each quarter offers legitimate discretion. Which comparables. Where in their range. What discount for illiquidity. Whether to reflect a soft quarter or wait for confirmation. Every answer is arguable.

And 1% a year of optimistic drift compounds to **+5.1% over five years**; 2% a year to **+10.4%**. Neither is detectable in any single quarter, and both are material to reported performance and to a fundraise.

So the detection has to be about pattern rather than about level:

**Do the discretionary choices ever go the other way?** A valuation process that has never produced an unexpected markdown is not exercising judgement.

**Has the methodology changed, and when?** Changes clustered before fundraises or after sector de-ratings are the pattern to look for.

**What do realisations achieve against final marks?** The single external check. Consistent exits above the last mark demonstrate conservatism; consistently below demonstrates the opposite.

**Is there a systematic gap between the marks and secondary market pricing?** [[secondaries|Secondaries]] are a real price for the same asset, and a persistent gap needs an explanation.

**The uncomfortable part: from inside a firm, drift is nearly invisible**, because each decision was made on its merits by people acting in good faith. It is only visible in the aggregate, over years, which is why someone has to be looking at the aggregate.
A fund with 1,000 of cost. One portfolio company: 80 of EBITDA, 400 of debt. The rest of the portfolio is held at cost, 700. Carry is 20% over cost.
walkthrough: **At a 9x multiple:** enterprise value 720, equity value 320. Fund NAV = 700 + 320 = **1,020**.
Gain over cost = 20. Accrued carry at 20% = **4.0**.
**At a 10x multiple:** enterprise value 800, equity value 400. Fund NAV = 700 + 400 = **1,100**.
Gain over cost = 100. Accrued carry at 20% = **20.0**.
**Read that carefully: one turn of multiple on a single holding multiplied accrued carry by five.** The valuation moved 8% and the manager's accrual moved 400%.
The mechanism is the threshold. Carry is charged on the amount above cost, so near the crossover point it is enormously levered to any valuation judgement.
**Which is why valuation governance should be tightest when a fund is close to its hurdle** — precisely when the temptation is greatest and the amounts are most sensitive.

Sanity check worth reusing: **before accepting any valuation change, compute its effect on accrued carry rather than on NAV.** The NAV effect is usually modest and the carry effect can be a multiple. That comparison identifies which valuation decisions carry real incentive pressure.

lesson.caption: What a valuation process should have
rows: Choosing the method that gives the answer
When was the methodology set, and has it changed?
Has the peer set changed since entry, and why?
A single person's judgement going unchallenged
Who can overrule the deal team, and have they?
Can I see the reason recorded for each change?
What did exits achieve versus final carrying value?

lesson.body:
**Deal teams valuing their own deals.** The people with the most information also have the most invested in the outcome. Independent review is not an insult to them; it is a control for a structural problem.

**Third-party valuation providers engaged narrowly.** A firm asked to confirm that a methodology was applied correctly is not the same as one asked whether the value is right.

**Auditors as a substitute for governance.** An audit tests whether the process was followed, not whether the judgement was good.

**Marks that never fall.** In any real portfolio some companies underperform. A book where nothing is written down is a statement about the process, not about the companies.

**Valuation timed around events.** Methodology changes or delayed markdowns near a fundraise, a continuation vehicle or a carry [[crystallisation]] date.

**Cross-fund transactions priced internally.** The manager sets the price and represents both sides. It can be done properly and it requires an external reference and independent consent.

**The most useful thing to understand about valuation ethics is that most of the people involved are honest, and the outcome can still be systematically wrong.**

That is uncomfortable, and it is why the framing "are they honest?" is the wrong question. Honest people, each making a defensible call in a system where every call has an incentive attached, will produce a biased aggregate. No individual has done anything they would be ashamed of.

So the questions worth asking are structural, and they are all answerable:

**Who can say no?** A valuation committee whose members are compensated on fund performance has no independent member.

**What is the record of being wrong?** A process that produces markdowns has demonstrated it can.

**Is the incentive visible to the person deciding?** A deal partner who knows their carry depends on this mark is in a difficult position, and acknowledging that is better than pretending otherwise.

**And what happens when a mark is challenged?** The response to a challenge tells you more about the culture than any policy document.

**For an allocator, the practical version is narrow: track realisations against final marks over several years.** It is the only external evidence, it requires no trust, and it accumulates into a genuine measurement of valuation discipline. **A manager who exits consistently above their last marks has proven something no policy statement can.**

**Compute any valuation change's effect on accrued carry, not just on NAV.** The carry effect can be a multiple of the NAV effect, and it identifies where the pressure is.

**Ask what exits achieved relative to final carrying values over the last three years.** The only external check, and it is a matter of record.

**Ask whether any peer set or methodology has changed since entry, and why.** Changes clustered around fundraises are the pattern.

**Ask who on the valuation committee is not compensated on fund performance.** If the answer is nobody, there is no independent voice in the room.

**Ask for an example of a markdown the committee imposed against the deal team's view.** A process that has never done this has not yet been shown to work.

items: Managers value their own portfolios because there is no market price — so the ethical content is in the process rather than in any single number.
One turn of multiple on one holding moved fund NAV 8% and accrued carry from 4.0 to 20.0, because carry is levered to the gain above a threshold.
The realistic failure is drift: 1% a year of optimism compounds to +5.1% over five years, invisible in any quarter and material to a fundraise.
Track realisations against final marks. It needs no trust, it accumulates over years, and it is the only external measurement of valuation discipline.

questions.stem: Why do private market managers value their own portfolios?
choices: Because regulation permits it and nobody has objected
Because there is no market price for a private company, so someone must estimate one — and the owner holds the most information
Because independent valuation is prohibitively expensive
rationales: It is permitted, and the reason it exists is the absence of an alternative rather than the absence of objection.
Correct. No quoted price exists, so a judgement is required, and the party with the best information is the owner. That is the structure rather than a loophole.
Third-party valuation services are widely used alongside the manager's estimate, not instead of it.
Investors would generally prefer an independent price and there is none available.
questions.explanation: Starting from the structural necessity keeps the discussion productive. The question is never whether the manager should value the portfolio — it is what process surrounds the judgement, and who can say no.

questions.stem: A fund cost 1,000. The rest of the portfolio is at cost (700) and one company is marked at 320 of equity value. What is accrued carry at 20% over cost?
questions.explanation: At a mark of 400 rather than 320 the same calculation gives 20.0 — five times as much. The NAV moved 8% and the carry moved 400%, because carry is charged on the gain rather than on the value.

questions.stem: Same fund, but the company is marked at 400 of equity value instead. What is accrued carry at 20% over cost?
questions.explanation: The fivefold jump from a one-turn valuation change is why governance should be tightest when a fund sits near its hurdle. That is where an arguable judgement has the largest effect on the decider's own compensation.

questions.stem: Why is the process around a private valuation more important than the number itself?
choices: Because the number is genuinely uncertain and two honest people can differ widely — so what distinguishes a sound valuation is whether the process would also produce lower numbers
rationales: It is uncertain rather than arbitrary — a range of defensible values exists and is bounded.
Correct. Since a range is defensible, "the mark is defensible" carries almost no information. What matters is whether the same process produces markdowns when those are the honest answer.
Audit scope is a consequence of the difficulty, not the reason process matters.
Investors can and do assess valuations; the constraint is information rather than capability.
questions.explanation: It leads to the most useful single question about a valuation process: show me a markdown the committee imposed against the deal team's view. A process that has never done that has not been demonstrated to work.

questions.stem: "Our valuation team is honest, so our marks are reliable." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — honest people each making individually defensible calls in a system where every call carries an incentive will produce a biased aggregate, and no individual will have done anything shameful
False — valuation teams are systematically dishonest
True — integrity of the individuals is what determines reliability
False — because valuations should be entirely outsourced
rationales: Correct. This is the structural point: the bias emerges from the aggregate of good-faith decisions each of which had an incentive attached. Individual honesty does not prevent it.
Over-correction and empirically wrong — most are honest, which is precisely why the structural framing matters.
Integrity is necessary and not sufficient, which is the whole content of the topic.
Outsourcing helps and cannot replace the manager's judgement, since the manager holds the information.
questions.explanation: Framing it structurally also makes the conversation easier to have. Asking "who can say no?" is a question about design; asking "are you honest?" is an accusation, and it produces defensiveness rather than information.

questions.stem: Why is valuation drift hard to detect from inside a firm?
choices: Because each individual decision was defensible and made in good faith — the bias is only visible in the aggregate over years
Because junior staff are excluded from valuation discussions
Because drift is not a real phenomenon
rationales: Internal data is available to the people making the decisions, which is why confidentiality is not the barrier.
Correct. 1% a year of optimism is invisible in any quarter and compounds to 5.1% over five years. Nobody experiences making a wrong decision.
They are often involved, and involvement does not make the aggregate visible.
The compounding arithmetic makes it entirely real and quantifiable.
questions.explanation: The consequence is that someone must deliberately look at the aggregate — a record of every discretionary choice and its direction. Nobody encounters that view in the ordinary course of work, which is why it has to be someone's explicit job.

questions.stem: As an allocator, which evidence about valuation discipline requires no trust in the manager?
choices: What realisations achieved relative to their final carrying values, over several years
The composition of the valuation committee
rationales: A policy states intent; it is not evidence of application.
Correct. A realisation produces an external price for the same asset, so the comparison with the prior mark is an objective measurement that accumulates over time.
Auditor quality matters for process assurance and does not measure valuation optimism.
Committee composition is informative about design and is still a structural claim rather than an outcome.
questions.explanation: It is the one metric in private markets where the market grades the manager's homework. Exits consistently above final marks demonstrate conservatism; consistently below demonstrates the opposite — and either way it is a matter of record rather than of assurance.
